📄 Unity forced enemy to accept Iran’s rights: Pezeshkian

📌 Tehran, IRNA – President Masoud Pezeshkian says Iran’s internal unity and cohesion compelled its enemies to surrender, accept the rights of the Iranian nation and return to the negotiating table.

Speaking on Sunday on the anniversary of the martyrdom of Mostafa Chamran in 1981 and the establishment of the Professors Basij Organization, Pezeshkian said that national solidarity had been the country’s greatest source of strength.
​
“Our unity and cohesion forced the enemy to surrender and brought them to the negotiating table,” he said.
​
The president said Iran must continue creating opportunities for the advancement of all members of society, adding that the world’s admiration and surprise at Iran’s stature stem from the people’s presence on the streets, their support for the government, and their refusal to stand against the country.
​
“The enemy did not believe in our internal unity and cohesion, and it was this unity that enabled us to achieve victory and forced them into dialogue,” he said.
​
The remarks came days after Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding to end the US-Israeli-imposed war against the Islamic Republic.
​
Pezeshkian and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, signed the agreement digitally and remotely on Wednesday.
​
The chief executive also warned that losing national solidarity would undermine the country’s progress.
​
“If we lose our unity and cohesion, we will get nowhere, because our most important strength is our unity with one another and our unity with the people,” he said.
​
He also praised the role of the Iranian people in managing the imposed war, saying it was the public’s Basiji spirit that helped secure victory.

Taiwan has accumulated $602 billion in foreign exchange reserves. But there's one serious problem: 80% of that amount is held in U.S. dollars.

That's why the country is now officially discussing the idea of converting part of those reserves into Bitcoin.

The reason: Taiwan effectively does not control its money. And it's unclear what could happen to those assets if China ultimately attacks the island and Taiwan faces a major crisis.

🔐 A new philosophy of reserves

In the past, countries held their reserves in gold and U.S. dollars. But after several nations discovered that their money could be frozen at a critical moment, attitudes toward reserve assets began to change.

And Bitcoin is different: it isn't held in another country's bank, it doesn't need to be physically transported, and it can't be blocked by a single political decision.
